item.title: The Mythical Man-Month in the Age of AI (149 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://j11g.com/the-mythical-man-month-in-the-age-of-ai, See on Hacker News

27 October 2026

Last weekend I watched four people desperately trying to get a laptop to connect to a screen. I was happily observing their efforts, with zero intent to join in.

But someone nudged me: can't you have a look at it?

My reply: "Haha sorry no! My experience is that adding more people will not solve this problem any quicker".

I was of course -- indirectly -- referring to Brooks's Law:

"Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later."

It was formulated by computer scientist Frederick P. Brooks Jr. in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month, based on his experience managing the IBM OS/360 project.

However I got to thinking. Does this still hold up in the age of AI agents and LLMs?

At first glance, you’d think no. The traditional bottlenecks -- onboarding time, endless stand-ups, and office politics -- disappear overnight. An AI agent is up to speed in milliseconds and doesn't demand a coffee break.

But when you look closer, and the law hasn't vanished. It just mutated.

The famous "Baby Problem" remains: nine agents still can’t deliver a baby in one month. Sequential tasks are still sequential.

Overhead hasn't disappeared; it shifted: instead of managing people, you are now managing agents. Someone still needs to define "done", review the code, catch hallucinations, and stitch the pieces together.

That someone is you.

Throw nine autonomous agents at a single codebase without crystal-clear orchestration, and they will happily rewrite each other's work in a high-speed loop.

Maybe the 2026 update to Brooks’s Law should be:

"Adding agents to a project with unclear requirements gets you the wrong answer faster."

item.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (155 responses) (138 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.cloudflare.com/kv-cache-exposure-remediation/, See on Hacker News

On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.

Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.

After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.

What happened

GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day.  

This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.

The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.

Immediate remediation

After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:

To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.

To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704, which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988, merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935, which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.

We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.

Background: how we serve GLM 5.3

Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via Mooncake, to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on high-performance LLMs and smaller, faster, safer models.

The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page).

Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do.

Issue one: misconfiguration

On our GLM 5.3 prefill nodes with our configuration, the pool came to 681,280 tokens while the model's context length is 1,048,576 tokens. The selected KV pool size is printed by SGLang in logs during startup and exposed as a metric. We were aware of this size mismatch; however, during pre-launch testing we observed successful HTTP status codes and a streaming body with no error frames during benchmarking. We assumed that the engine was capable of gracefully handling the difference between the KV cache pool and requested context window via streaming or some other mechanism.

This was one critical gap in our testing: we only validated HTTP response codes and engine performance at long contexts, without validating model output and coherence. We now check KV pool size against context length directly, from the running engine, before any disaggregated deployment change ships, rather than inferring it from response codes.

Issue two: SGLang bug

In v0.5.21, the SGLang team has now addressed this bug in how it was handling prompts longer than the KV pool size. Here’s what was happening before.

When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. The rejection path (Req.set_finish_with_abort) recorded the error to be returned to the client and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder so that the request could drain through the normal batch machinery without allocating real memory. On a single-node deployment this worked: the placeholder ran, the batch finished, and the client received an error.

In disaggregated mode such as we operate, the admission queues on both prefill and decode checked whether a request was finished, not whether it was rejected. A rejected request reported itself as live. So:

  1. Bootstrap. The router told the decode node the prompt length (8 pages in the diagram). Decode reserved 8 KV pages for the request.
  2. Prefill admission. The prefill admission queue admitted any request where req.finished() was False. A rejected request stored its rejection in to_finish, not finished_reason, so finished() still returned False. The rejected request was admitted.
  3. Prefill forward pass. Rejection had already replaced the prompt with a one-token placeholder. Prefill ran a trivial forward pass on that one token.
  4. KV transfer. Prefill sent one page of KV to decode and signaled that the transfer was complete.
  5. Decode admission. Decode's admission queue had the same finished() check, so it accepted the handoff.
  6. Decode attention. Decode started generating and attention read all 8 reserved pages. Only page P0 had been written by this request. Pages P1 to P7 still held what earlier requests left in them: other users' prompts and partial generations.
  7. Response. The client got HTTP 200 instead of HTTP 400. prompt_tokens matched the long prompt and the reply was coherent. It arrived faster than an 8-page prefill should take, and it contained content from other users' KV pages.

Every request over the threshold behaved this way. This bug had been reported to SGLang by another user as issue #30233 on July 6, 2026, which Cloudflare noticed while investigating this incident. We had been flagging these types of issues with SGLang since v0.5.10 and this security incident sped up work that Cloudflare had already started in collaboration with the SGLang team. The patch for this issue was released in SGLang v0.5.20, with follow-ups in v0.5.21 and v0.5.22, and is available for all other operators dependent on SGLang to use. We highly recommend all operators update SGLang dependencies to v0.5.22 or later. For more details on specific PRs, read on below.

GLM 5.3 was the only model affected by this bug. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We have applied the engine fix and the hardening described below to every model we serve with SGLang, and our deployment checks require them for every new deployment.

Timeline

All times UTC.

When

What

Aug 27, 2026

GLM 5.3 launched on Workers AI with a prefill KV pool smaller than its context window. The exposure was present from launch.

Sep 8, 2026 - 23:11

Report received via HackerOne.

Sep 9, 2026 - 08:00

Cloudflare begins verifying the HackerOne report.

Sep 9, 2026 - 13:22

Security incident declared. Product Security reproduced the leak using two independent accounts within 25 minutes.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:00

After confirming the scope of the issue, GLM 5.3 was set to private. Requests return HTTP 400. Status page updated.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:35

Root cause identified as the prefill pool being smaller than the context length. Canary prefill node with a larger pool confirmed not susceptible.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:52

All prefill nodes rolled to the corrected configuration.

Sep 9, 2026 - 19:04

Full deployment rebuilt with the corrected configuration plus a Cloudflare-authored engine patch that correctly returns errors for requests rejected by the prefill scheduler. Validated against the researcher's reproduction script.

Sep 9, 2026 - 19:40

Model restored to public.

Sep 10, 2026 - 23:30

Meeting with the SGLang maintainers (RadixArk CTO and core engineers) to agree on upstream fixes.

Sep 11-19, 2026

Additional hardening rolled to all production SGLang deployments (details below).

Sep 16-Oct 12, 2026

Upstream SGLang merges the admission fix, per-transfer checksums, abort-ACK preservation, and turns deferred KV release on by default.

Oct 2, 2026

SGLang v0.5.21 released.

Oct 19, 2026

SGLang v0.5.22 released.

Oct 26, 2026

Coordinated publication with the researcher and RadixArk.

Ongoing hardening effort

This bug belongs to a class of KV cache memory-safety bugs that Cloudflare has been working to address for several months. In each case, a page is freed, reused, or read while something else still has a claim on it. We see two common causes.

The first is page lifetime within a single node. Several tasks on a decode node can hold the same page at once: token generation, offload to host memory, the KV transfer receiver, and the abort and error paths. If one of them frees the page while another is still using it, a new request can be given that page while it is still being read or written. Our earlier fixes for decode offload (#24226, #30899) and double release on grammar errors (#30937) were of this kind.

The second is a race across nodes. When a request is aborted while prefill is still writing its KV cache to decode over RDMA, the writes already sent cannot be recalled. If decode frees those pages right away, those pages can be given to another request, and the late writes land in that request's KV cache. Cloudflare has contributed to the effort to fix this race through proposed fixes (#31357, #38961) and a reproduction script (#32564). In both cases the result is corrupted output, or one user's data in another user's response, with no error raised. The bug in this incident was different: a rejected request went through the handoff every time, rather than by a timing accident. But it had the same result: decode reading pages this request never wrote. None of these covered the failure in this incident in which prefill rejected the request, and decode never learned of it.

Since the incident, we have:

  • Extended deferred release to hold prefill's source pages as well, and to cover every failure type, not just aborts. We proposed it upstream as #38961, which was superseded by #40645, #41402, and #41404.
  • Deployed bounded Mooncake transfer batches (#32758, from the SGLang community), so no single transfer call can outlast the release timeout.
  • Changed our load balancer so a client disconnect no longer aborts a request mid-transfer. It holds the prefill connection until prefill finishes and the decode connection until the first token, then closes both.
  • Added a check to every disaggregated deployment change: KV pool size measured against context length, deferred release on both roles, transfer batch bounds inside the release timeout, and all required patches applied.

All of these changes were released to our disaggregated production deployments.

Working with the SGLang team

We met with the SGLang maintainers at RadixArk on September 10, the day after the incident. We agreed that RadixArk would investigate the race conditions we had reported, upstream the integrity-checking idea, and build reproduction tests for this class of bug.

The following have landed on SGLang main to address this incident and related KV cache race conditions, and all but one are included in v0.5.22. Operators running disaggregated SGLang should update to v0.5.22 or backport these patches as needed.

These follow-ups are still works in progress:

  • #39729 Additional cleanup for --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum. Merged, awaiting release.
  • Zero KV pages on release, draft proposal: #46435
  • Extend KV checksum validation from the prefill-to-decode handoff to every decode step (see Integrity by construction, below)
  • Broader KV Canary and KV Checksum model and feature support

What we recommend to other operators

If you run SGLang in disaggregated prefill/decode mode, we recommend the following:

  1. Measure your KV pool and compare it to your context length, on every prefill and decode node, from the engine's startup log, after every change to weights, quantization, parallelism, or memory fraction. If the pool is smaller, lower the context length to fit. Do not rely on a proxy to enforce the limit, and do not assume the engine will reject what does not fit. This is the check we did not enforce.
  2. Upgrade to a build that includes #36988 and #38935 (v0.5.22 or later), so an over-length request is rejected before handoff regardless of pool size. This is the engine-side fix, and it is the backstop for the day your check in step one is wrong.
  3. Run with deferred KV release on both roles (default after #41023), and bound your Mooncake transfer batches so a single timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded tail of writes.
  4. Turn on corruption detection where your model supports it. --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum and --kv-canary do not yet cover every model architecture. Check your logs to confirm requests are being verified. We are working with the SGLang team to extend both checks to more architectures, including GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.
  5. Ensure your proxy is not generating unnecessary aborts. Configure your load balancer to allow requests to proceed up to the first token, so that you do not trigger an abort that requires cross-node coordination.

Longer term

Integrity by construction

Configuration checks and lifecycle fixes reduce the number of ways a page can be misused. They do not make misuse impossible, and this incident is a reminder that the next bug will have a shape we have not seen. The durable answer is for the engine to detect, at read time, that a request is about to attend over a page it does not own, and fail that one request rather than return someone else's data.

We built a prototype of this over the summer and described it in August. Every physical KV page carries a tag that changes when the page is reallocated, each request records the tags it expects, and the mapping is checked before decode reads the cache. In our tests it cost under 1% in throughput and tail latency. We tested it on GLM 5.2 in mid-August, but disabled it shortly afterwards due to reliability issues.

The prototype was also tied to specific attention backends and model architectures, so it could not be a general fix. We are working with the SGLang team to build a production version into the engine that works across every model, rather than maintaining Cloudflare-specific patches. The per-transfer checksum in #39500 is a first step: it validates the handoff from prefill to decode. Page-level tags go further, because they check every read, including reads long after the transfer.

Integrity by mathematical impossibility

RDMA copies data directly from one node’s memory to another’s. It’s vital for the two machines to agree on where the data goes, how large it is, and when it’s finished; any mismatch can cause the receiver to read the wrong data. This bug is an example of a consistency failure in a distributed system, in which the two machines had inconsistent views of the state of that system.

Elsewhere in Cloudflare, we have put effort into proving the safety of distributed systems using formal verification methods. Topaz enables conflict-free IP selection for our authoritative DNS servers. Models of Meerkat’s QuePaxa implementation have demonstrated consistency bugs that were subsequently fixed.

We are now directing our experience in formal methods to KV cache transfer engines. This will start with modeling and proving the safety of an RDMA-based KV cache transfer protocol. The goal is to model our production SGLang’s distributed KV cache system using Mooncake, then track and fix any divergence from the safety properties we want to guarantee. The aim is to prove — as far as possible — that a bug like this cannot occur again. Realistically, we expect gaps in what the provers can tell us, but proving the rest of the system allows us to more closely review and monitor those gaps.

Coordinated disclosure

We are publishing this report as part of a coordinated disclosure. We want to thank the researcher, Gadi Evron, who reported this through our HackerOne program with a clear, reproducible script and gave us time to fix it and to coordinate with the SGLang maintainers before publishing. We also want to thank the SGLang team at RadixArk, who treated this as their problem as well as ours and landed the upstream fixes with urgency.

Read more at the post from the SGLang team.

If you find a security issue in Workers AI, please report it at hackerone.com/cloudflare.

item.title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to a quarter of its workforce (123 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.kuow.org/technology/2026-10-26/microsoft-offers-voluntary-buyouts-to-a-quarter-of-its-workforce, See on Hacker News

Published October 26, 2026 at 10:16 AM PDT

Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees in an effort to further reduce its headcount.

Chief People Officer Amy Coleman sent a memo to employees Monday detailing the terms of the voluntary exit offer, which will be available to roughly one quarter of Microsoft’s workforce.

“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,” Hood said in the memo. “It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs.”

The buyouts will be available to select employees in the U.S., U.K., Canada, and India at level 70 and below in the company’s ranking system. That ceiling applies to the vice president level at the company.

A Microsoft spokesperson said the offer will be comparable to the company’s standard severance package, which varies by market but typically includes base pay for a certain amount of time (based on tenure), stock options granted over time, health care, and career planning services.

The exit offer comes a few months after Microsoft offered voluntary early retirement to employees of a certain tenure at level 67 and below. About 30% of eligible employees took that offer, though Microsoft expects this broader round of buyouts to have a smaller adoption rate. That’s, in part, because the voluntary retirement program offered more generous terms to incentivize uptake.

Eligibility for the new program was determined by the heads of each organization at Microsoft. That means the sales organization, some corporate services like marketing, and some engineering teams will not be participating.

The spokesperson said artificial intelligence is not driving the buyout programs. Microsoft has, however, been on an employee-cutting spree for several years as it invests billions of dollars into the infrastructure needed to train and run AI models.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. … There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee,” Hood said in the memo. “These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.”

item.title: Somebody please stop the spam texts (137 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://notes.npilk.com/stop-the-spam-texts, See on Hacker News

Summary: I complain about spam texts and consider why I’m so hesitant to just reply STOP to unsubscribe.

I moved out of Texas a few years ago. Unfortunately, it doesn’t seem like any statewide midterm candidates have heard about that. In the past month, I’ve gotten dozens of texts like this, usually multiple per day:

Some of the texts I received while working on this post

They seem to be mostly from Republicans, but I’ve gotten a little bit of everything — texts from Democrats, independents, PACs, unbiased pollsters, obviously biased pollsters, even those weird false flag texts that went around. I don’t remember signing up for anything, and certainly would never have intended to, but clearly my number got on a list somehow.

This is pretty annoying, because text is my highest-signal communication channel. Most of what’s in there is from family and friends, plus the occasional 2FA code. The little red notification bubble means a lot more on Messages than other apps — which of course is exactly why politicians, marketers, and scammers want so badly to get in there.

It’s not just the elections, either — this has been getting noticeably worse over time. This year I’ve started to get a ton of these types of messages, sometimes as many as one a day:

It turns out, despite seeming all personal and handwritten, that if you reply STOP, these messages also reveal themselves to be part of a larger campaign. (Shouldn’t this be illegal, by the way?)

So it seems like the solution is to reply STOP to all of these and eventually you won’t get as many, right?

Except I haven’t done that. I don’t want to do that. Except for that “experiment” above, I have instead chosen “Delete and Report Spam” for every single one of these texts… even though it doesn’t seem to do anything.

What’s crazy to me is that Apple has actually added a Spam folder to Messages, and there are a few things in there. But even though I’ve been reporting all this stuff as spam for months, if not longer, none of the new messages I get seem to get filtered into the Spam folder.

So again, why not just reply STOP to these messages? Why am I so averse to doing that?

After some reflection, I think I figured it out: replying with STOP feels like I’m accepting this vision of the world.

If I reply STOP, I’m basically saying, “Okay, you’re allowed to send me whatever you want, and then I have to send back STOP for you to knock it off.” And I want to fundamentally reject that framing. Mass-texting and spam campaigns shouldn’t get that right by default, and the burden shouldn’t be on me to individually opt-out of every single one of these campaigns.

So if you’re reading this and you work on iOS at Apple, please help. This feels like a great use case for all this new Apple Intelligence (similar to the AI adblock experiment I ran a while back). If I report something as Spam, maybe an option could pop up to “Filter messages like this to Spam?” or something, and then the unwanted text gets added to a list of examples. So then next time I get a text from an unknown number, the LLM reads the list of spam examples, and if the new message is similar, it goes to Spam. (That’s just off the top of my head; I’m sure there are even better ideas to combat this.)

Recently, I did find a “Delete and Stop” option, which auto-sends the STOP message for me. But it seems like “Delete and Stop” and “Delete and Report Spam” are mutually exclusive. You’d think that reporting as spam would also auto-send a STOP message, but the number of texts I’ve gotten from Don Huffines despite reporting each one suggests otherwise.

Hopefully things will calm down after the election. But for goodness’ sake, somebody please do something about this. I was going to say we fixed this problem for email, but I’m not really sure we did — these days I get tons of marketing messages despite always trying to opt out on every single website whenever I purchase something. And I get multiple spam calls a day too, even though I’m on the Do Not Call registry. So maybe we’re just doomed to be eternally pestered by whoever wants our money or our vote. Here’s hoping they don’t figure out how to get into my Slack. ⧈

item.title: The EPA Is Quietly Killing Its Web Archive (284 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.motherjones.com/environment/2026/10/epa-online-archive-deletion-zeldin-camp-lejeune-trump-clean-power/, See on Hacker News

Screenshot of the Environmental Protection Agency's homepage.Mario Guti/Getty

Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs. Sign up for the free Mother Jones Daily.

In a little-noticed webpage update, the Environmental Protection Agency has announced a plan to decommission its online web archive at the end of the year, a move that would wipe tens of thousands of publicly available environmental resources from the web. The discreet banner notice comes in stark contrast to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin’s recent public takedowns of the agency’s power plant pollution standards and federal methane regulatory system.

“The EPA’s online archive makes information about a wide variety of environmental issues and past policies available to the public, dating back at least 20 years,” said Gretchen Gehrke, co-founder of the Environmental Data and Governance Initiative (EDGI). “This information is irreplaceable, and if the archive is decommissioned, that information will be lost forever.”

For decades, the web archive has been an unparalleled resource for researchers, legislators, policymakers, and the public writ large. It houses everything from fact sheets and environmental reports to agency policy changes and regulatory actions, making it a tool for “democratic oversight,” according to Gehrke, who for ten years has been tracking changes to vulnerable federal environmental data.

This isn’t the first time the environmental agency has tried to shutter the online web archive. In late January 2022, the Biden administration EPA announced plans to discontinue the online repository, citing burdensome financial upkeep; through a Freedom of Information Act request, Gehrke was able to determine that the agency spent roughly $2 million a year to maintain it. A coalition of environmentalists, historians, and librarians swiftly condemned the decision, with groups like the EDGI and American Society for Environmental History calling the announcement “alarming” and cause for a “tremendous gap” in the historical record. 

After five months of public backlash, the EPA acquiesced, in part by announcing it would delay the web archive’s retirement by one year to July 2023. I reported on it at the time for New Security Beat: 

“News of this welcome reprieve for the EPA digital archive raises a significant question: Why continue with plans to shut it down at all? Postponement does not resolve the eventual damage to government transparency and historical record keeping that the archive’s demise will create. And the concern of organizations opposed to closure will not be satisfied by an additional year of operation.” 

In March 2023, the agency walked back its decision further still by adjusting the banner announcement to say that the online web archive was simply “retiring”—end date not included. Since then, over the last three and a half years, the online resource has soldiered on quietly, no longer being updated, but still accessible to the public. Until a few weeks ago, when the EPA updated the archive’s expiration date to December 31, 2026. 

While the usability of the archive has historically been far from perfect—researchers often encountered dead links and frustratingly limited search capabilities—the archive has held a trove of tens of thousands of EPA documents dating back to the 1990s simply not available elsewhere.

Major political environmental inflection points could be tracked through the archive, such as President George W. Bush’s 2003 Clear Skies Initiative, or President Barack Obama’s 2015 Clean Power Plan—two initiatives that sought to dramatically transform power plant pollution standards. And during President Trump’s first term, when the administration deleted the majority of the EPA’s climate change web resources, the online resource crucially maintained and made accessible these defunct pages for the public. 

The archival repository has also been a tool for environmental enforcement and oversight. In 1989, after an investigation found that military operations had contaminated the soil, sediment, surface water, and groundwater at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune and the Marine Corps Air Station in North Carolina, the EPA listed the base on its National Priorities List. Documents on the EPA’s decades-long investigation were preserved on the archive and helped nearby residents and service members on base overcome doubts about the agency’s effectiveness and better evaluate chemical exposures. Earlier this week, President Trump said he would withhold compensation due to service members and their families exposed at Camp Lejeune if Republicans lose their majority in Congress.

Now, the EPA’s latest move could further undermine public confidence at a time when trust in government is near historic lows. 

“The EPA’s insistence on decommissioning its web archive will only continue to erode public trust—at the exact time the public and lawmakers need agency information the most,” Lauren Harper, the first Daniel Ellsberg chair on government secrecy for the Freedom of the Press Foundation, wrote in an email. “Killing easy access to records forces researchers and lawmakers to flood an already underwater FOIA office just to see once-public records.”

The recently updated webpage states that historical information can still be found in the EPA’s “snapshot collections,” but given the second Trump administration’s crusade against public data and evisceration of funds to federal programs and personnel, it’s hard to know for sure if all, or even a fraction, of the archive’s contents will live on. 

“EPA should expand and systematize the archive, not throw it away and expect that three discrete snapshots will suffice,” said Gehrke. 

The EPA did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Type Server Protocol (244 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/microsoft/pylance-release/blob/main/docs/tsp/type-server-protocol.md, See on Hacker News

The Type Server Protocol (TSP) is a JSON-RPC protocol for asking a type server for Python analysis data. A type server maintains the type-analysis state for a workspace and answers requests for the protocol version, snapshots, Python search paths, import resolution, and type queries (computed, declared, and expected types).

The protocol uses Language Server Protocol (LSP) data shapes and conventions where they are useful, such as Position and Range, and it represents URIs as strings the same way LSP does. TSP methods use the typeServer/ prefix.

The protocol artifacts in this folder are the authoritative definitions:

  • typeServerProtocol.ts defines the TypeScript interfaces and request types.
  • tsp.json is the machine-readable protocol model.
  • tsp.schema.json is the JSON schema for the protocol model.

Version History

TSP uses semantic version strings for client/server compatibility checks. While the protocol is in the 0.x line, minor version changes may be breaking. Patch version changes remain backward compatible within the same minor line.

Version Changes
0.1.0 Initial protocol version.
0.2.0 Added request types and fields.
0.3.0 Switched to more complex type shapes.
0.4.0 Switched to the Type union and stub-based type payloads.
0.4.1 Added multi-connection negotiation and the typeServer/connection control request.

Connection Model

A client starts a type server and communicates with it over the main JSON-RPC connection using a transport the server supports, such as stdio or Node IPC. When using stdio, stdout must be reserved for JSON-RPC protocol messages.

A type server is expected to receive enough workspace and document state to answer the TSP requests it supports. Clients commonly use normal LSP initialization and document synchronization for this state, then send typeServer/* requests on the same JSON-RPC connection.

TSP also supports optional extra read-only connections. The original connection remains the main connection and owns initialization, workspace state, document synchronization, state-changing notifications, and connection control. Extra connections are opened only after client and server negotiate support during initialization.

Startup Sequence

A typical session follows this order:

  1. The client starts or connects to the type server.
  2. The client and server initialize any shared workspace state, commonly through the LSP initialize and initialized messages.
  3. The client calls typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion and verifies that the returned semver string is compatible with the protocol version it expects.
  4. The client calls typeServer/getSnapshot to obtain the first snapshot identifier.
  5. The client sends type-query, import-resolution, or search-path requests that include the current snapshot when required by the request shape.
  6. The server sends typeServer/snapshotChanged when prior type results are no longer valid.

Multi-Connection Mode

Multi-connection mode is an optional performance feature. It lets a client open additional local channels to the same type server for read-only TSP requests, while the main connection continues to own the mutable workspace state.

Clients should use multi-connection mode only when they can benefit from concurrent read-only work, such as high-volume type queries or background workers that should not block the main JSON-RPC connection. A server must still work correctly in single-connection mode. Multi-connection support must not be required for protocol correctness.

Capability Handshake

Multi-connection support is negotiated through the normal LSP initialize request and response. A client that can open extra TSP channels advertises the supported transport kinds under capabilities.experimental.typeServerMultiConnection:

{
    "capabilities": {
        "experimental": {
            "typeServerMultiConnection": {
                "supportedTransports": ["ipc"]
            }
        }
    }
}

A server that can serve extra TSP channels returns the same capability shape in the initialize result:

{
    "capabilities": {
        "experimental": {
            "typeServerMultiConnection": {
                "supportedTransports": ["ipc"]
            }
        }
    }
}

Multi-connection mode is enabled only when both sides advertise typeServerMultiConnection and the two supportedTransports lists have at least one transport in common. If either side omits the capability, or if there is no common transport, the session remains single-connection and the client must not send typeServer/connection.

The currently supported built-in transport kind for extra connections is ipc. This negotiation is separate from the main connection, which can use stdio or Node IPC.

Opening An Extra Connection

After initialization and transport negotiation, the client opens an extra channel by sending typeServer/connection on the main connection:

{
    "type": "open",
    "kind": "ipc",
    "args": ["<ipc-endpoint>"]
}

For ipc, the args array identifies the endpoint or endpoints that the server should connect to. The server should validate the request, connect to the supplied endpoint promptly, and return a result with success: true when it accepts the request. If the server cannot open the channel, it should return success: false and include a short message when useful for logs.

IPC Endpoint Arguments

An ipc endpoint is expected to provide a full-duplex JSON-RPC stream when the platform IPC mechanism supports it. In that case, args contains one endpoint string:

{
    "type": "open",
    "kind": "ipc",
    "args": ["<full-duplex-ipc-endpoint>"]
}

If the platform IPC mechanism exposes only one-way endpoints, args contains two endpoint strings. The endpoint names are from the type server's perspective: the first endpoint is the server input stream, and the second endpoint is the server output stream.

{
    "type": "open",
    "kind": "ipc",
    "args": ["<input-ipc-endpoint>", "<output-ipc-endpoint>"]
}

Closing An Extra Connection

The client closes an extra channel by sending typeServer/connection on the main connection with the same transport kind and endpoint identity:

{
    "type": "close",
    "kind": "ipc",
    "args": ["<ipc-endpoint>"]
}

The server should stop serving the matching extra channel and close the transport promptly. A client may also tear down its local transport if the server does not complete the close within the client's timeout budget.

The close request should use the same args shape that opened the channel: one endpoint for a full-duplex IPC stream, or the same input/output endpoint pair for a split IPC stream.

Allowed Traffic

The main connection owns all state-changing traffic. The following must remain main-connection-only:

  • LSP initialization and lifecycle messages.
  • Workspace, configuration, file-watcher, and document synchronization notifications.
  • Server-to-client snapshot notifications.
  • The typeServer/connection control request.

Extra connections are TSP-only and read-only. They may be used for requests that do not mutate server state and whose results are valid for the snapshot supplied by the client.

The allowed TSP messages on an extra connection are bound to the negotiated TSP version. If a server reports support for a TSP version and advertises multi-connection support for that session, it must support every extra-connection TSP message defined for that version.

The table below lists the TSP version that first allows each message on an extra connection:

TSP version Extra-connection message
0.4.1 typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion
0.4.1 typeServer/getSnapshot
0.4.1 typeServer/getPythonSearchPaths
0.4.1 typeServer/resolveImport
0.4.1 typeServer/getComputedType
0.4.1 typeServer/getDeclaredType
0.4.1 typeServer/getExpectedType

Servers should reject LSP traffic, state-changing notifications, typeServer/connection, and any TSP message not allowed for the negotiated TSP version when received on an extra connection.

Snapshots

A snapshot is a non-negative integer that identifies a point-in-time view of the type server's analysis state. Type handles, declarations, symbols, and other returned objects are valid only for the snapshot in which they were returned unless a request explicitly says otherwise.

The type server must advance the snapshot whenever a previously returned type-analysis result may be invalid. Typical invalidating events include opened-file changes, closed files, configuration changes, watched-file changes, dependency changes, or any cache reset that changes analysis results.

Snapshot rules:

  • typeServer/getSnapshot returns the current snapshot identifier.
  • Snapshot identifiers must not decrease during a session.
  • typeServer/snapshotChanged reports the previous and new snapshot identifiers.
  • Requests that include a stale snapshot should fail with a JSON-RPC error that lets the client retry with a fresh snapshot. LSP's ServerCancelled error code (-32802) is the preferred error for this case.

Positions And Ranges

TSP follows LSP position conventions:

  • Lines are zero-based.
  • Character offsets are zero-based UTF-16 code units.
  • Ranges identify source spans using a start position and end position.

If a type server stores source locations in another encoding, it must convert locations at the protocol boundary. Incorrect conversion can cause the client to request information for the wrong syntax node.

Nodes, Declarations, And Handles

The type-query requests (typeServer/getComputedType, typeServer/getDeclaredType, typeServer/getExpectedType) identify a source construct with an arg that is either a node or a declaration. A node is a URI plus a source range. A declaration describes where and how a symbol is defined and is either a regular declaration, which is backed by a source AST node, or a synthesized declaration, which is created by the type checker and has no source node.

InvalidHandle is -1 and represents an invalid or unavailable handle. Clients and servers should treat it as a sentinel value, not as a valid object identifier.

Type Results

Type results are JSON-serializable tagged objects. Each type includes a discriminator that tells the client how to interpret the rest of the object. The protocol supports built-in types, declared types, functions, classes, unions, modules, type variables, overload sets, synthesized types, and type references.

Every type object carries a numeric kind discriminator, a numeric id, and a bitfield of flags:

kind Type Description
0 BuiltIn unknown, any, unbound, ellipsis, never, and similar
1 Declared Base for source-declared types (rarely used directly)
2 Function Functions and methods from def statements
3 Class Classes and their instances
4 Union Union types (int | str | None)
5 Module Module objects (import os produces a Module type for os)
6 TypeVar Type variables (T, P, Ts)
7 Overloaded Functions with multiple @overload signatures
8 Synthesized Types synthesized by the type checker
9 TypeReference Reference to another type by id, used for deduplication and cycles

Type objects are snapshot-bound, and type IDs are response-local:

  • A returned type object is valid only for the snapshot used by the request that produced it.
  • Type IDs are used to connect TypeReference objects to earlier type objects in the same serialized response graph.
  • Type IDs are not a stable global identity for a snapshot and should not be compared across separate responses.
  • Type references should be used to avoid duplicating large or recursive type graphs within one response.

Protocol Surface

The current protocol is intentionally small. The exact parameters and result shapes are defined in the protocol artifacts; the table below lists every TSP message with its direction and payload shape.

Message Direction Params Result
typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion client → server none string (semver)
typeServer/getSnapshot client → server none number
typeServer/snapshotChanged server → client { old: number, new: number } notification
typeServer/connection client → server { type: "open" | "close", kind, args? } { success, message? }
typeServer/getPythonSearchPaths client → server { fromUri, snapshot } string[] | undefined
typeServer/resolveImport client → server { sourceUri, moduleDescriptor, snapshot } string | undefined
typeServer/getComputedType client → server { arg: Declaration | Node, snapshot } Type | undefined
typeServer/getDeclaredType client → server { arg: Declaration | Node, snapshot } Type | undefined
typeServer/getExpectedType client → server { arg: Declaration | Node, snapshot } Type | undefined

A type server should implement the messages required by the client it integrates with and return undefined only where the protocol's result type allows it.

Type Queries

The three type-query requests differ by which type they report for the same node or declaration:

  • typeServer/getComputedType returns the type inferred from code flow. After narrowing a to int, the computed type of b in b = a + 1 is int.
  • typeServer/getDeclaredType returns the type explicitly written in the source. For def foo(a: int | str), the declared type of a is int | str.
  • typeServer/getExpectedType returns the type the surrounding context expects. For the call foo(4), the expected type of the argument is int | str.

Error Handling

Use standard JSON-RPC error responses.

Situation Error code Guidance
Stale snapshot -32802 (ServerCancelled) The client can request a fresh snapshot and retry.
Invalid parameters -32602 (InvalidParams) Required fields are missing or malformed.
Internal failure -32603 (InternalError) The server failed unexpectedly while handling a valid request.

Errors should include enough message detail for a client log to identify the failed request, but they should not expose local secrets or implementation-only state.

Compatibility Checklist

A compatible type server should verify these behaviors:

  1. typeServer/getSupportedProtocolVersion returns a semver string supported by the client.
  2. All request and notification payloads serialize and deserialize according to the protocol artifacts.
  3. typeServer/getSnapshot returns a non-negative snapshot and snapshots do not go backward.
  4. Document, configuration, and watched-file changes invalidate snapshots when they can change returned analysis data.
  5. Requests with stale snapshots fail with a retryable cancellation error.
  6. Position and range conversions use LSP zero-based UTF-16 conventions.
  7. Import-resolution requests return document URIs or no result according to the protocol result type.
  8. Type queries (computed, declared, and expected) return well-formed Type objects, or undefined, for the snapshot supplied by the client.
  9. Multi-connection support is advertised only when the server can serve the negotiated extra transport.
  10. Extra connections accept every TSP request allowed for the negotiated TSP version and reject LSP traffic, state-changing notifications, typeServer/connection, and TSP requests not allowed for that version.

by ICL Noticias

Employees at Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, have expressed concern over what they describe as “obvious” and “biased” favoritism toward members of the Bolsonaro family during Brazilian elections.

In a statement, the company’s workers held Meta’s leadership responsible for decisions that, they argue, could undermine the credibility of the democratic process.

Brazilians protest in front of the Meta building in London, UK, against the company’s interference in Brazil’s presidential elections. (Brasil Matters)

The statement was signed by members of the tech sector branch of the United Kingdom’s Communication Workers Union, CWU. In the text, the employees voice concern regarding recent revelations about the company’s management and point to the risk of interference in the elections of other nations.

“Since 2016, the political leanings of Meta executives and company leaders has been no secret,” the document states.

The employees emphasize, however, that they consider this systematic and user-perceptible application of political favoritism to be unprecedented.

“But this is the first time to our knowledge that favours made to politicians such as the Bolsonaros have been programmatically made user-facing to such an obvious and biased extent,” the statement reads.

The text also expresses concern that the company’s actions could damage public trust in democratic institutions and in digital platforms themselves.

“The last thing we want is to sit back and watch our employer interfering in the democratic processes of countries like Brazil,” the employees say.

According to the group, a loss of credibility in elections and politicians could also erode trust in the technologies developed by the company. The employees warn that this scenario sets a dangerous precedent for the future.

“We Meta employees want to build technologies and platforms that millions of people use and enjoy,” the text states. “In undermining the credibility of elections and politicians, it also unfairly undermines the credibility of what we build, and sets an incredibly dangerous precedent for the future.

At the end of the statement, the employees call on the company to respect democratic principles.

“We call for fairness and democracy to be respected,” the document concludes.

On Saturday, October 24, a protest against Meta’s interventions in the Brazilian elections took place in front of the company’s headquarters in King’s Cross, central London. The demonstration was organized by the “Alliance for Democracy and Brazilian Sovereignty,” a collective of movements bringing together Brazilians in England.

Brazilians protest in front of the Meta building in London, UK (Annaís Berlim/Brazil Matters)

Below is the full text of the statement:

As employees of Meta, we are disturbed by the revelations of the past few days and weeks regarding our management.

Since 2016, the political leanings of Meta executives and company leaders has been no secret.

But this is the first time to our knowledge that favours made to politicians such as the Bolsonaros have been programmatically made user-facing to such an obvious and biased extent.

We Meta employees want to build technologies and platforms that millions of people use and enjoy.

The last thing we want is to sit back and watch our employer interfering in the democratic processes of countries like Brazil.

In undermining the credibility of elections and politicians, it also unfairly undermines the credibility of what we build, and sets an incredibly dangerous precedent for the future.

We call for fairness and democracy to be respected.

item.title: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11 (433 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.enlyth.com/posts/oldest-windows-gui-app-win-11/, See on Hacker News

Early investigation

For a while I’ve been wondering about a silly question, which is, what’s the oldest application with a GUI that will still run on Windows 11 without modifications or emulation.

Given Windows’ excellent backwards compatibility, I expected the answer to be something impressively old.

Sadly, Windows 11 can’t run 16-bit Windows programs by itself, because 64-bit Windows has no NTVDM, so we’re going to have to find something from the early NT era.

I remember asking this question a while ago on an anonymous forum, where someone pointed me to Win32s, and suggested to find an early release version of it with FREECELL.exe.

So I did exactly that, and lo and behold, FREECELL.EXE with a date modified of 22-Feb-93 running and fully playable, without any changes on the latest version of Windows 11:

At the time of this post, that’s a 33 years and 8 months old application, which is impressively almost as old as me.

So I kinda thought “cool”, considered this a solved mystery and forgot about it shortly afterwards. But for some reason, this question popped into my mind again lately and this time I decided to dig deeper to see if I can find something older.

Further efforts

Digging through old Windows versions on the Internet Archive, I found some early NT 3.1 pre-release versions that seemed promising, but the main issue seemed to be either incompatibility with today’s executable format or API changes that came later in development.

The earliest 1991 versions used a draft PE format not compatible with modern Windows, and builds up to mid-1992 assumed the cdecl calling convention instead of stdcall for Windows API calls, so arguments would get removed twice, as such:

push hwnd          ; 4 bytes of args
call [ShowWindow]  ; Win11 ShowWindow is stdcall, ends with "ret 4" and removes them
add  esp, 4        ; the 1992 caller removes them again

Which would understandably cause the program to crash.

There was one application that caught my eye though, from Build 347, and that was CDPLAYER.EXE, linked on 16-Nov-1992. By then the calling convention was fixed, but the other programs in that build crash in their bundled C runtime. CDPLAYER.EXE avoids that by using the system’s crtdll.dll, and Windows 11 still ships a crtdll.dll in SysWOW64.

If you start the program, you get something like this:

That is because, duh, my computer doesn’t have a CD-ROM drive. But you can use a small DLL (cdemu.dll) to emulate one with some fake audio data and actually get it to play audio:

Pretty cool for a program that’s almost 34 years old!

What if we cheat?

So earlier I mentioned that 16-bit programs are out of the picture because they are no longer supported.

But if you want, you can use something like otvdm to run older Windows applications.

Behold, a fully playable version of REVERSI.EXE dated 15-Nov-1985 running on Windows 11, taken from Windows 1.01:

And although using otvdm does feel like cheating, I thought it was cool enough to include in this post.

He also said his wife advised him to never apologize, said he would prefer to never do interviews with the press again, and claimed without evidence that the social media opposition to Flock is driven mostly by Russian bots.

“Somebody was paying for [the social media posts and] stopped paying for it,” Langley said about the many viral posts criticizing his company’s technology. “Social media chatter on Flock is down about 95 percent from July. It went down 50 percent last week when Ukraine bombed a Russian data center with a drone. Literally 50 percent overnight. And so look, I’m the last person, my wife as well, she’s like ‘This is crazy, these people are getting paid to say these things,’” he added, repeating a disproven theory that Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers had a significant impact on internet bot activity. 

“It’s anonymous bots, and so it is not real,” he continued. “Inorganic activity has led to organic activity, but when I look at protests across the country, it is the same people with the same signs and the same message. That’s not normal. That’s not organic at all.” Langley’s comments echo another unsubstantiated theory that said opposition to Flock comes from a far-left network spreading propaganda at the behest of China.

Langley made the comments at the International Association of Chiefs of Police (IACP) conference, which is running Saturday to Tuesday in Orlando, Florida. Many law enforcement contractors exhibit at the conference, and speakers get to attend with more than 16,000 public safety officials.

Flock makes automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) and other surveillance cameras. Its ALPRs constantly scan the license plate, color, make, and model of every vehicle that drives past, creating a timestamped log of peoples’ movements. The embattled company has faced extensive media and public scrutiny as instances of police abuse, false arrests, and the use of the technology for immigration enforcement have come to light. Dozens of cities have canceled their contracts with Flock over the last 18 months. 

As backlash to the company grew, Langley began doing damage control with the media, which included apologizing for calling DeFlock, a group that maps the location of Flock cameras, a “terroristic organization.” In the audio from the IACP conference, Langley suggested that he generally should not apologize for the company.

“I give my wife a lot of credit. She was, like, you should never apologize,” Langley said. “Sure, people make mistakes. I've made a lot of mistakes in the last nine years. I made a lot of mistakes this summer. But we do good work.”

The session itself was framed as a fireside chat between Langley and David Rausch, IACP’s president and director of the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation. The schedule said the session would “examine the opportunities, challenges, and public debate surrounding the technology [ALPRs], including issues related to privacy, transparency, governance, data use, and community trust.” 

Flock makes the ALPR data available to its law enforcement customers, who can query it without a warrant. Flock differentiates itself from other ALPR providers, like Axon, by providing a national network of ALPRs. A cop in one part of the U.S. can search cameras not just in their own jurisdiction, or even state, but all over the country, if those other police departments have added their cameras to the network. A recent count put the national network at around 80,000 cameras.

That national network is a large part of why Flock has faced so much criticism. 404 Media revealed last year that local cops were doing lookups in Flock for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and a cop in Texas searched cameras nationwide for a woman who self-administered an abortion.

Langley said he’d like to not do any more media interviews. “The media gets to say whatever they want to say about you,” he said.

I’m going to try to figure this out but I think for me, I wish we could do this more often and you know I’m excited about the work we’re doing together and think we have a lot of ideas to continue to make up,” Langley said. 

404 Media’s investigations on Flock and others have triggered a nationwide conversation about whether individual communities want Flock cameras stationed on their roads or inside their children' s gymnastics class.
